title_en: Hong Kong Xinjianye Co., Ltd. et al. v. Shanghai Xinjianye Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over debt guarantee
keywords_en: civil; debt guarantee dispute; second instance; Supreme People's Court; Shanghai; Hong Kong Special Administrative Region; Macao Special Administrative Region; legal person; natural person; Contract Law; validity of applicable law clause; exercise of powers before registration of change of legal representative; validity of guarantee contract; affirm the original judgment; equity transfer; debt guarantee; change of legal representative; guarantee; debt guarantee dispute involving Ye Co., Ltd. and others
full_text_en:
Hong Kong New Development Limited et al. v.

Shanghai New Development Limited et al. — dispute over debt and guarantee

[Ruling Summary]

1. Where parties to a foreign-related economic contract in writing separately agree upon or confirm the choice of law clause, such clause shall be confirmed as valid in accordance with the law.

2. Even if the legal representative of an enterprise has been removed from office but has not yet completed the registration of the change with the government enterprise registration authority, such person may still exercise the corresponding powers externally, provided that doing so does not violate the interests of the enterprise.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2001) Min Si Zhong Zi No. 13

Appellants (Defendants at First Instance): New Construction Property Development (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. Domicile: No. 2438, Zhongshan North Road, Putuo District, Shanghai.

Legal Representative: Tan Ruichun, General Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Zang Jun, Attorney at Beijing Long An Law Firm.

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): Hong Kong Wei Cheng International Co., Ltd. Domicile: Room 1808, 18/F, Tower 1, Lippo Centre, 89 Queensway, Central, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Legal Representative: Li Xishun, Director of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Yang Jingang, Staff Member of the Company.

Appellees (Plaintiffs at First Instance): New Construction Property and Real Estate (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. Domicile: Rooms 402-3, 4/F, 10-16 Gough Street, Central, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Legal Representative: Shen Zhubang, Director of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Cen Wenqi, Attorney at Shanghai Jingrui Law Firm.

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): Senda Development Co., Ltd. Domicile: 11/F, Blocks A and B, Yide Commercial Building, Beijing Street, Macao Special Administrative Region.

Legal Representative: Li Rujin, Director of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Chen Rongquan, Director of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Dai Bin, Attorney at Guangdong Huafa Law Firm.

The appellants, New Construction Property Development (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Shanghai New Construction Company) and Hong Kong Wei Cheng International Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Wei Cheng Company), appealed to this Court against the civil judgment (1999) Hu Gao Jing Chu Zi No. 4 rendered by the Shanghai High People's Court regarding the dispute over debt and guarantee with the appellees, New Construction Property and Real Estate (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Hong Kong New Construction Company) and Senda Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Senda Company). This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel composed of Judge Wang Yun as Presiding Judge, and Acting Judges Chen Jizhong and Ren Xuefeng as members, and held a public hearing of this case on January 23, 2003. The agent ad litem of appellant Shanghai New Construction Company, Zang Jun, the legal representative of appellee Hong Kong New Construction Company, Shen Zhubang, and its agent ad litem, Cen Wenqi, and the agents ad litem of appellee Senda Company, Chen Rongquan and Dai Bin, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. Appellant Wei Cheng Company, having been duly served with summons by this Court, failed to appear in court without justifiable reasons. This case is now concluded.

The facts found by the court of first instance are as follows:

1. On January 25, 1995, Hong Kong New Construction Company, Wei Cheng Company, Shen Zhubang, Wu Lisheng, Liang Shusen, and New Construction Property (Macau) Co., Ltd. jointly entered into a contract (hereinafter referred to as the Transfer Contract). Its main contents were: Hong Kong New Construction Company, Shen Zhubang, Wu Lisheng, and Liang Shusen, as registered shareholders of Xinfa Asia Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xinfa Company), undertook to transfer the 9,000 issued shares of Xinfa Company held by them to Wei Cheng Company, and also to allot the 200,000 unissued shares of Xinfa Company to Wei Cheng Company; in consideration, Wei Cheng Company was to pay a consideration for the allotment of HK$79,793,000, of which HK$10 million was to be paid before the signing of the contract and the balance was to be paid to Hong Kong New Construction Company on or before January 30, 1995. Meanwhile, with respect to Shanghai New Construction Company, in which Xinfa Company held an investment, the transferee Wei Cheng Company was also to assume a debt of HK$246,123,516.78 owed by Xinfa Company to the share transferors. Hong Kong New Construction Company was to sell a loan of HK$48,236,567.83 to Wei Cheng Company for HK$1. Accordingly, Wei Cheng Company was to pay a total of HK$277,679,948.95. If any claims or other disputes arose under this contract, Hong Kong law would apply, and the parties would submit to the jurisdiction of the High Court of Hong Kong, provided that such jurisdiction was not exclusive. The above contract was confirmed by a notarial certificate issued by a Hong Kong lawyer recognized by the Ministry of Justice, and its contents conform to Hong Kong law.

2. On January 17, 1997, Hong Kong New Construction Company, Wei Cheng Company, and Senda Company entered into the "Supplemental Agreement on Payment for Shanghai New Construction Center" (hereinafter referred to as the Payment Supplemental Agreement), stipulating that, pursuant to the Transfer Contract, the repayment plan was confirmed as follows: Hong Kong New Construction Company was to complete the procedures for the transfer of property rights and title, including the legal representative of Shanghai New Construction Company, all property certificates and shares, etc., before January 22, 1997; Wei Cheng Company was to use Shanghai New Construction Center as a guarantee for repayment; Wei Cheng Company was to repay HK$10 million to Hong Kong New Construction Company before February 3, 1997, and to pay the remaining balance in installments before July 22, 1997, and to make such payments on behalf of Hong Kong New Construction Company to Senda Company. This Supplemental Agreement was signed by Wu Lisheng and Liang Shusen on behalf of Hong Kong New Construction Company, Li Chen on behalf of Wei Cheng Company, and Chen Rongquan on behalf of Senda Company, and witnessed by Deng Weihua. On October 8, 1998, Hong Kong New Construction Company, Wei Cheng Company, Senda Company, and Nanhai Xiqiao Economic Development General Company (hereinafter referred to as Xiqiao Company) entered into the "Explanation (I) on Clause 2 of the Supplemental Agreement of January 17, 1997" (hereinafter referred to as "Explanation (I)"), clarifying that from the signing of the contract on January 25, 1995 to the date of signing the Payment Supplemental Agreement, Wei Cheng Company had paid approximately HK$160 million to Hong Kong New Construction Company, with an outstanding balance of approximately HK$110 million. Because Hong Kong New Construction Company owed Senda Company and Xiqiao Company a debt of HK$70 million, in order to resolve the long-standing debts among the three parties, Hong Kong New Construction Company assigned a claim of HK$70 million to Senda Company or its wholly-owned subsidiary Xiqiao Company; Wei Cheng Company agreed to pay the HK$70 million to Senda Company; the remaining HK$40 million was still to be repaid by Wei Cheng Company to Hong Kong New Construction Company. The above "Explanation (I)" was signed by Wu Lisheng, Liang Shusen, and Shen Zhubang, affixed with the seal of Hong Kong New Construction Company, and signed by Li Chen on behalf of Wei Cheng Company, and affixed with the seals of Senda Company and Xiqiao Company. On the same day, Hong Kong New Construction Company, Wei Cheng Company, and Senda Company further entered into the "Explanation (II) on Clause 2 of the Supplemental Agreement of January 17, 1997" (hereinafter referred to as "Explanation (II)"), clarifying that Wei Cheng Company had paid approximately HK$160 million to Hong Kong New Construction Company, with an outstanding debt of HK$110 million; Hong Kong New Construction Company agreed to assign a claim of HK$70 million to Senda Company; Senda Company confirmed that it had received HK$5 million in 1997, with an outstanding balance of HK$65 million; the three parties agreed that Shanghai New Construction Company would serve as the guarantor for repayment and would enter into relevant guarantee agreements. Hong Kong New Construction Company, Wei Cheng Company, and Senda Company affixed their seals to confirm the above "Explanation (II)."

3. On January 20, 1997, Shanghai New Construction Company, Senda Company and Xiqiao Company, and Hong Kong New Construction Company entered into a "Mortgage Guarantee Contract," specifying that Shanghai New Construction Company would use Shanghai New Construction Center as collateral for the guarantee of Wei Cheng Company's repayment, with the guaranteed repayment amount being HK$110 million (interest at the Hong Kong prime rate for January 1997 plus 2). Shanghai New Construction Company was the guarantor for repayment; when the debtor failed to repay on time, the creditor could register the collateral at any time; this contract and the "Guarantee Deed of Mortgage" would take effect simultaneously. The next day, Xiqiao Company, Senda Company, Xinfa Company, and Shanghai New Construction Company entered into a "Work Memorandum," confirming the Payment Supplemental Agreement of January 17, 1997, specifying the use of Shanghai New Construction Center as a mortgage for repayment, and stipulating that the interpretation of any agreements subsequently signed would be ultimately defined by the Chinese language and Chinese law. On January 23 of the same year, the above parties entered into a "Guarantee Deed of Mortgage," stipulating that the mortgagor was Shanghai New Construction Company, the mortgaged property was the real estate located at No. 2438, Zhongshan North Road, Shanghai, the mortgage amount was HK$110 million, and the interest rate was prime plus 2. On February 25 of the same year, Shanghai New Construction Company, Senda Company, Xiqiao Company, and Hong Kong New Construction Company entered into a "Surety Contract," specifying that Shanghai New Construction Company was willing to assume the responsibility of guaranteeing Wei Cheng Company's repayment, the guaranteed amount was HK$110 million plus interest, liquidated damages, compensation, etc., and the guarantee period was until all debts were finally fully settled. Each of the above contracts bore the contract-specific seal of Shanghai New Construction Company, and Shen Zhubang signed the contracts in his dual capacity as the representative of both Shanghai New Construction Company and Hong Kong New Construction Company.

4. Xinfa Company was incorporated and registered in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, with an authorized capital of HK$2,009,000. In 1995, it had issued 9,000 shares, with shareholders being Hong Kong New Construction Company, Shen Zhubang, Wu Lisheng, and Liang Shusen. On February 5, 1997, the 9,000 issued shares of the company were transferred to the name of Wei Cheng Company. On January 22, 1997, the company issued an additional 2,000,000 new shares, of which 1,979,910 shares were transferred to the name of Wei Cheng Company and 20,090 shares to the name of Yin Jun (a director of Wei Cheng Company). In 1994, Xinfa Company established Shanghai New Construction Company, a wholly foreign-owned enterprise in Shanghai, which obtained a land lease to develop the plot at No. 2438, Zhongshan North Road. On January 18, 1997, Shanghai New Construction Company held a board of directors meeting, deciding to remove Shen Zhubang from his positions as chairman and general manager, and appointed Yin Jun as chairman and general manager. At that time, the directors of Shanghai New Construction Company were Liang Shusen, Yin Jun, Wu Lisheng, Li Chen, Shen Zhubang, and Yang Xueli. On April 4, 1997, the documents and the company seal (excluding the above contract-specific seal) of Shanghai New Construction Company were handed over to Wei Cheng Company. On June 27, 1997, upon approval by the industry and commerce registration authority, the legal representative of Shanghai New Construction Company was changed from the original Shen Zhubang to Yin Jun of Wei Cheng Company.

5. Pursuant to the 1995 Transfer Contract, up to the time of signing the Payment Supplemental Agreement, Wei Cheng Company had paid a total of HK$149,680,944.01 to Hong Kong New Construction Company. Adding HK$20,944,551.65 that Hong Kong New Construction Company confirmed having received (including returns on principal already received and deductions for the 25th floor proceeds), the total payment amounted to HK$170,625,495.66. From January 1997 to before July 22, 1997, Wei Cheng Company paid HK$7,000,000, and after July 22, 1997, paid an additional HK$710,092. The remaining balance was not paid by either Wei Cheng Company or Shanghai New Construction Company.

6. After the signing of the Mortgage Guarantee Contract, the Surety Contract, and other documents, various entities, including the Xiqiao Mountain Tourism Resort District People's Government, sent multiple letters to Shanghai New Construction Company and Wei Cheng Company demanding timely repayment. Wei Cheng Company also undertook to repay the amounts to Senda Company.

On April 19, 1999, Hong Kong New Construction Company and Senda Company jointly filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance concerning the dispute over debt and guarantee, requesting a judgment ordering Wei Cheng Company to pay an outstanding debt of HK$109,404,733.65 and to compensate for interest of HK$29,423,548.20, and ordering Shanghai New Construction Company to assume joint and several liability for satisfaction. On August 10, 2000, Hong Kong New Construction Company and Senda Company amended their claims to request a judgment ordering Wei Cheng Company to pay an outstanding debt of HK$108,689,230 and to compensate for interest of HK$35,914,260 (from May 1, 1996 to April 30, 2000), and ordering Shanghai New Construction Company to assume joint and several liability.

On April 20, 1999, upon the application of Hong Kong New Construction Company and Senda Company for preservation of property, the court of first instance, by the civil ruling (1999) Hu Gao Jing Chu Zi No. 4, sealed up all the properties on the first to tenth floors and the twenty-first to twenty-fourth floors of the Shanghai New Construction Center building owned by Shanghai New Construction Company.

During the defense period after service of the statement of claim, Wei Cheng Company and Shanghai New Construction Company both raised objections to jurisdiction, arguing that the contract of January 25, 1995 stipulated that "this contract shall be interpreted under and governed by Hong Kong law; the parties to this contract agree that any disputes or claims arising under this contract shall be adjudicated by the Hong Kong court." The creditor and debtor in this case were both Hong Kong legal persons, and Shanghai New Construction Company was merely a guarantor, so the case should be under the jurisdiction of the court of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. Upon review, the court of first instance held that "the full meaning of the contract is: this contract shall be interpreted under and governed by Hong Kong law; the parties to the contract agree, without dispute, that any claims and disputes arising under this contract are subject to the jurisdiction of the High Court of Hong Kong, but it is also stated that it does not have exclusive jurisdiction." On this basis, the court of first instance rejected the jurisdictional objection. The two defendants were dissatisfied and appealed to the Supreme People's Court, which held that: "The parties have no dispute over the equity transfer contract of January 25, 1995. The clauses in that contract cannot restrict Hong Kong New Construction Company and Senda Company from filing the present action based on the Payment Supplemental Agreement entered into with Wei Cheng Company and the Mortgage Guarantee Contract and Guarantee Deed of Mortgage entered into with Shanghai New Construction Company, on the ground of a dispute over debt and guarantee. Since these three contracts all stipulate the application of mainland law and contain no agreement on jurisdiction clauses, the Shanghai High People's Court has jurisdiction."

The Shanghai High People's Court, upon trial, held: The focus of the dispute between the plaintiffs and the defendants was whether the Payment Supplemental Agreement and the guarantee agreements were valid. 1. Regarding the validity of the Payment Supplemental Agreement. This agreement was a repayment plan confirmed based on the contract of January 25, 1995. The plaintiffs confirmed that the reference to the "contract of January 25, 1995" in the Payment Supplemental Agreement actually referred to the contract signed by the six parties mentioned above. The defendants' argument that the contract referred to in the Payment Supplemental Agreement did not exist had no factual basis. From the signing of that contract to the date of signing the Payment Supplemental Agreement in January 1997, Wei Cheng Company had paid HK$149,680,944.01, which far exceeded the total price of HK$79.793 million that Wei Cheng Company argued was the consideration for acquiring the equity of Xinfa Company and the Shanghai New Construction Company project. Moreover, in the Payment Supplemental Agreement and the explanations, Wei Cheng Company repeatedly confirmed that it had paid approximately HK$160 million, with an outstanding balance of approximately HK$110 million, and undertook to repay Senda Company. Therefore, the plaintiffs' claim that the transfer fees were approximately HK$270 million was credible. The defendants' defense that no debt existed was inconsistent with the established facts and was not accepted. Neither the Payment Supplemental Agreement nor the subsequent "Explanation (I)" or "Explanation (II)" specified a definite amount of the outstanding debt; they merely confirmed that the outstanding debt was approximately HK$110 million. During the trial, it was determined that the actual outstanding debt at that time was HK$107,054,452.34 (HK$277,679,948 - HK$170,625,495.66), which was consistent with the agreement of the relevant parties. This amount could be confirmed. The Payment Supplemental Agreement was signed by Li Chen, a director of Wei Cheng Company, on behalf of Wei Cheng Company. Furthermore, in the subsequent "Explanation (II)" signed by both parties, Wei Cheng Company affixed its seal for confirmation. Therefore, it could be determined that the Payment Supplemental Agreement represented the true intention of Wei Cheng Company. Additionally, the other rights holders under the contract of January 25, 1995 (including Shen Zhubang, Wu Lisheng, and Liang Shusen) all confirmed the Payment Supplemental Agreement, agreeing that their claims against Wei Cheng Company would be repaid to Hong Kong New Construction Company by Wei Cheng Company. Thus, the Payment Supplemental Agreement and the related explanations were lawful and valid. Although defendant Wei Cheng Company argued that Hong Kong New Construction Company and Senda Company had engaged in malicious collusion and civil fraud, it did not provide corresponding evidence, and this argument was not accepted. 2. Regarding the performance of the contract and the assumption of liability. After the Payment Supplemental Agreement was signed, all parties were required to strictly perform it. The plaintiffs had transferred and allotted the shares of Xinfa Company to Wei Cheng Company and had handed over the relevant documents and seals of Shanghai New Construction Company, thereby fulfilling their delivery obligations. Wei Cheng Company only paid HK$7,710,092, leaving an outstanding balance of HK$99,344,360.34 unpaid. Its conduct clearly constituted a breach of contract, and it should bear the liability for paying the remaining amount and default interest. The plaintiffs claimed interest from May 1995 at the Hong Kong prime rate plus 2. Upon review, neither the contract of January 25, 1995 nor the Payment Supplemental Agreement specifically stipulated the interest rate or the starting date for calculating interest. The actual performance of contractual obligations by the parties was mainly concentrated in 1997. Therefore, the plaintiffs' claim lacked factual and legal basis. The default interest should be calculated from after the final repayment date of July 22, 1997, as determined in the Payment Supplemental Agreement, at the overdue loan interest rate of the People's Bank of China for the corresponding period. Hong Kong New Construction Company assigned part of its claim to Senda Company, which, upon confirmation by the company, acquired that part of the claim. Since the two plaintiffs requested that their respective claims not be divided in this case, the court, in accordance with the plaintiffs' wishes, declined to divide their co-tenancy claims, leaving them to be divided by the two plaintiffs themselves after the judgment. 3. Regarding the validity and liability of the mortgage contract, guarantee contract, etc. Shanghai New Construction Company argued that the contract-specific seal of Shanghai New Construction Company affixed to the mortgage contract, guarantee contract, and other agreements was privately engraved by the plaintiffs, and therefore, these agreements were all forgeries. The court held that Shen Zhubang was then the legal representative of Shanghai New Construction Company and had control over the company seal and could directly sign contracts externally. Therefore, objectively, there was no need for the plaintiffs to secretly engrave the seal. The failure of the original Shanghai New Construction Company to hand over this seal at the time of transfer did not preclude the lawful existence of the seal at that time. Moreover, Shanghai New Construction Company did not provide further evidence that the plaintiffs had privately engraved the seal. Thus, this defense of Shanghai New Construction Company was not accepted. After the mortgage contract was signed, the mortgage registration procedures were not completed to date. Therefore, the mortgage contract was not effective under the law. The existing evidence also could not prove that either party was at fault for the ineffectiveness of the contract. Therefore, the contract had no legally binding force on either party. The "Surety Contract" was signed by Shen Zhubang on behalf of Shanghai New Construction Company and affixed with Shanghai New Construction Company's contract-specific seal. At the time of signing, although Shen Zhubang had been removed from his position as legal representative by the board of directors, the industrial and commercial registration had not yet been changed. Legally, he could still represent Shanghai New Construction Company in expressing its intent externally. The guarantee of Shanghai New Construction Company's property was consented to by its former controlling shareholder, Hong Kong New Construction Company, and its subsequent controlling shareholder, Wei Cheng Company. Although Shanghai New Construction Company did not form a board resolution regarding the guarantee, most of its board members signed the relevant agreements, confirming Shanghai New Construction Company as the repayment guarantor. The guarantee contract arose because the debtor had not paid the full transfer price, which could have rendered the creditor's claims uncollectible. Therefore, the creditors, to avoid risk, used the transferred subject matter as collateral to achieve self-relief. This was a relatively reasonable method that could be adopted at the time and was consistent with the principle of fairness. Moreover, there was currently no explicit legal prohibition against such conduct. In summary, it was determined that the "Surety Contract" represented the true intention of Shanghai New Construction Company and should be valid. Since the contract did not specify the form of guarantee, Shanghai New Construction Company should assume joint and several liability for satisfaction.

Accordingly, the court rendered the following judgment in accordance with Article 84 and Article 111 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 19, Article 41, and Article 42 of the Security Law of the People's Republic of China: (1) Weicheng Company shall, within ten days from the effective date of the judgment, pay Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company the outstanding amount of HKD 99,344,360.34 and overdue interest (calculated from July 23, 1997, to April 30, 2000, at the loan interest rate of the People's Bank of China for the corresponding period); (2) Shanghai Xinjianye Company shall bear joint and several liability for the above repayment obligation. The case acceptance fee of RMB 754,799.89 shall be borne by Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company in the amount of RMB 111,869.99, and by Weicheng Company in the amount of RMB 633,929.90; the property preservation fee of RMB 736,309.89 shall be borne by Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company in the amount of RMB 110,446.48, and by Weicheng Company in the amount of RMB 625,863.41.

Shanghai Xinjianye Company and Weicheng Company, dissatisfied with the original judgment, appealed to this court, arguing: (1) Pursuant to the contract between Weicheng Company and Hong Kong Xinjianye Company regarding the acquisition of all equity interests in Xinfa Company, the acquisition price was HKD 79,793,000, and Weicheng Company had fully paid all amounts due under the contract, thus fulfilling its payment obligations under the contract. The amount of indebtedness of HKD 107,054,452.34 as determined in the original judgment had no factual or legal relationship whatsoever with Weicheng Company or Shanghai Xinjianye Company. Shanghai Xinjianye Company should not bear any so-called guarantor liability, and Shanghai Xinjianye Company and Weicheng Company were not parties to this litigation. (2) The original judgment had already found that the so-called contract seal of Shanghai Xinjianye Company was not recorded with the Administration for Industry and Commerce, and Hong Kong Xinjianye Company did not deliver such seal to Weicheng Company at the time of transfer. Although new agreements were made regarding the equity interests of Xinfa Company and Shanghai Xinjianye Company, the relevant formalities and legal representatives were not handed over. Therefore, any civil acts of the company and its legal representative prior to April 1997, when the transfer formalities for the equity transfer were being conducted, could not represent either Weicheng Company or Shanghai Xinjianye Company, whose equity interests were partially acquired by Weicheng Company. The security arrangement set up by Hong Kong Xinjianye Company for the transfer of Shanghai Xinjianye Company had no legal effect, and Hong Kong Xinjianye Company could not assert rights against Weicheng Company by first placing the transferred assets as collateral. (3) The finding in the original judgment that "after the mortgage contract was signed, the mortgage registration procedures have not been completed to date; therefore, the mortgage contract has not taken effect, and there is no evidence to prove that either party to the contract was at fault for the non-effectiveness; Shanghai Xinjianye Company shall bear joint and several liability" was erroneous. First, the mortgage had no legal effect without registration. Second, the guarantee given by Hong Kong Xinjianye Company over Shanghai Xinjianye Company before transferring Shanghai Xinjianye Company was unrelated to the Shanghai Xinjianye Company after Weicheng Company acquired the equity interests. Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and its legal representative naturally could not express the intent of Shanghai Xinjianye Company externally. Weicheng Company only held a partial equity interest in Xinfa Company and had no right to externally create security over the assets of Shanghai Xinjianye Company. Therefore, the appellees were at fault for the non-effectiveness of the contract, and the guaranty contract was not the true expression of intent of Shanghai Xinjianye Company. Shanghai Xinjianye Company should not bear any liability. (4) Shanghai Xinjianye Company had never agreed to or ratified the creation of any security over its assets. According to the articles of association of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, Shen Zhubang had been removed from his position by a board resolution at the time of performance of the equity transfer contract in dispute and had no authority to represent Shanghai Xinjianye Company. If it were determined that the removed Shen Zhubang could still represent Shanghai Xinjianye Company, then it should be determined that the equity transfer agreement had not been actually performed, and at the same time, the creditor's right arising from the equity transfer would not exist, and the basis for the so-called guarantor liability of Shanghai Xinjianye Company would also be lost. All guarantee, surety, and mortgage contracts and agreements signed by Shen Zhubang, representing the interests of the original shareholder of Shanghai Xinjianye Company before the equity transfer, namely Hong Kong Xinjianye Company, constituted malicious fraud and were obviously unfair, and had no legal effect whatsoever. (5) The contract between Weicheng Company and Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and other parties expressly provided that disputes arising from the performance of the contract would be governed by Hong Kong law. After the court of first instance exercised jurisdiction over this case, if interest was to be calculated on the alleged outstanding amount, it should be done based on the actual circumstances of the case and after distinguishing the responsibilities of each party; interest should not have been calculated, and the judgment to calculate interest at the overdue loan interest rate of the People's Bank of China for the corresponding period lacked legal basis. (6) Pursuant to the Security Law, the guaranty contract in this case did not specify a guarantee period, and the parties engaged in fraud and malicious collusion. Shanghai Xinjianye Company should not only not bear joint and several liability, but should also be exempt from guarantor liability. They requested that the original judgment be reversed and the claims of Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company be dismissed.

At the second-instance hearing, the appellant Shanghai Xinjianye Company argued: The security involved in this case constituted an external security that was not approved or registered and should be void; the guaranty contract in this case was signed by Shen Zhubang, a director of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, using the company's assets to provide a guarantee for the company's shareholder, and the creditor was aware of this, so it should be void under the law; Shen Zhubang, the signatory of the guaranty contract in this case, simultaneously represented both parties in the same civil security transaction, constituting a typical "dual agency" that clearly harmed the legitimate rights and interests of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, and should be void under the law; after Shen Zhubang was removed as chairman of the board of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, he still fraudulently used the name of Shanghai Xinjianye Company to provide a guaranty, and Hong Kong Xinjianye Company, knowing this, still signed the guaranty contract with him; therefore, the guaranty contract should be deemed void. Accordingly, Shanghai Xinjianye Company should not bear any civil liability.

Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company responded: (1) The transfer contract was provided to the court by Weicheng Company, and the signatories to the contract were six parties: Weicheng Company, the appellee Hong Kong Xinjianye Company, and four other persons not involved in the case (Shen Zhubang, Wu Lisheng, Liang Shusen, and Xinjianye Property (Macau) Co., Ltd.). Weicheng Company claimed that the contract had been fully performed, but in the payment supplementary agreement, it acknowledged the fact of the debt and the method of repayment. Both Explanatory Notes 1 and 2 to the payment supplementary agreement were signed by Li Chen, a director of Weicheng Company, who acknowledged the debt of approximately HKD 110 million. The "Entrusted Financing Agreement" dated December 1, 1998, was signed by Li Chen, director of Weicheng Company, and bore the company seal, acknowledging the debt. The above evidence proves that Weicheng Company was a party to the contract. In all evidence submitted by the appellees to the court of first instance, there were accounting records showing Weicheng Company's repayment of the debt to the appellees, which were confirmed on September 12, 1998. Therefore, Weicheng Company's denial that it was a party to this case is erroneous. (2) In the payment supplementary agreement, Weicheng Company promised to use the Shanghai Xinjianye Center as security for repayment. Explanatory Notes 1 and 2 to the payment supplementary agreement both stated "... still owes HKD 110 million," again clarifying that Shanghai Xinjianye Company would serve as the repayment guarantor, and related guarantee agreements were signed. The Mortgage Guaranty Contract, Work Memo, Mortgage Guaranty Letter, and Guaranty Contract all clearly stated that Shanghai Xinjianye Company was willing to provide a guarantee for Weicheng Company's debt of approximately HKD 110 million, using its property, the Shanghai Xinjianye Center Building, as security and undertaking repayment responsibility until all debts were ultimately cleared; otherwise, they would voluntarily bear all legal responsibilities. On July 9, 1999, in its appeal to the Supreme People's Court against the first-instance ruling on jurisdiction, Shanghai Xinjianye Company publicly stated that this case was a dispute over a debt and guarantee, and that Shanghai Xinjianye Company was merely a guarantor. The above facts fully prove that Shanghai Xinjianye Company was the guarantor, and the Shanghai Xinjianye Center was the security. Regardless of whether the guarantee was valid, it should bear guarantor liability. Therefore, Shanghai Xinjianye Company is a party to this case. (3) The equity transfer price in the contract consisted of three parts, totaling HKD 277,679,948, not just the allotment consideration price of HKD 79,793,000. Weicheng Company had already confirmed the debt of approximately HKD 110 million. Therefore, the original judgment's determination that the actual debt at the time was HKD 107,054,452.34 is correct. (4) The Guaranty Contract was premised on the payment supplementary agreement and other agreements signed between Weicheng Company and Hong Kong Xinjianye Company. The date approved by the Administration for Industry and Commerce for the change of chairman of the board of Shanghai Xinjianye Company to Yin Jun was June 27, 1997. According to regulations, "the date of approval by the state administrative organ is the effective date of the change registration." Before June 27, 1997, Shen Zhubang was fully capable of directly signing contracts externally on behalf of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, and there was no need to privately engrave a seal. At the time of transfer, Shen Zhubang, concerned that Weicheng Company might not fulfill its repayment obligation, did not hand over the seal, but this does not preclude the lawful existence of the seal at that time. Therefore, Shanghai Xinjianye Company's claim that "the contract seal was privately engraved by Shen Zhubang" lacks legal evidence, and the court of first instance correctly found that the Guaranty Contract represented a genuine expression of intent and was validly formed. (5) China's Security Law provides that the exemption of guarantor liability is limited to the scope of the creditor's waiver of the creditor's right, which in this case refers to the portion of the creditor's right secured by the Shanghai Xinjianye Center Building that the creditor waived. Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company have never made any expression of intent to waive these real rights claims. The conditions for the guarantor to be exempt from civil liability under Article 30 of the Security Law are "the parties to the principal contract collude to defraud the guarantor into providing the guarantee; or the creditor of the principal contract uses fraud, coercion, or other means to cause the guarantor to provide the guarantee contrary to its true intention." Shanghai Xinjianye Company and Weicheng Company have not provided any factual basis for alleged malicious collusion. (6) This lawsuit was filed based on the payment supplementary agreement and the Mortgage Guaranty Contract, Mortgage Guaranty Letter, Guaranty Contract, and other debt and guarantee matters. These contracts all stipulate that the laws of the People's Republic of China shall apply. The application of law in the original judgment is correct. They requested that the appeal be dismissed and the original judgment be upheld.

Upon retrial, this court finds: The transfer contract is not a matter in dispute between the parties to this case, and this court does not confirm the facts concerning the transfer contract as determined in the original judgment. After cross-examination at the second instance, the appellant Shanghai Xinjianye Company raised objections to the fact determined in the original judgment that Weicheng Company had paid part of the amount, but did not provide corresponding evidence to overturn the corresponding facts already determined in the original judgment. Therefore, except for the facts concerning the transfer contract, this court confirms the other facts determined in the original judgment.

This court further finds: On January 21, 1997, Xiqiao Company and Senda Company, as Party A, and Xinfa Company and Shanghai Xinjianye Company, as Party B, signed a Work Memo, Article 5 of which stipulated: "All agreements signed mainly concerning the sale and purchase of the Shanghai Xinjianye Center and all agreements signed based thereon with representatives including Shanghai Xinjianye Company, Senda Company, Xiqiao Company, Hong Kong Xinjianye Company, and Xinfa Company: including all creditors and debtors. Since the collateral is located within China, the parties unanimously agree that with respect to all agreements, contracts, mortgage documents, powers of attorney, etc. signed, there may be inconsistent interpretations of some terms, and there may be different expressions of meaning in Chinese and English. Therefore, from the signing of this memo, all interpretations shall be finally defined by the Chinese language and Chinese law."

On October 8, 1998, the "Explanatory Note (2)" jointly signed by Hong Kong Xinjianye Company, Weicheng Company, and Senda Company stipulated in Article 2: "The three parties unanimously agree that Shanghai Xinjianye Company shall be the repayment guarantor, and shall sign the Mortgage Guaranty Contract, Work Memo, Mortgage Guaranty Letter, Guaranty Contract, and related documents, which shall complement each other to ensure the full implementation of Article 1 of this Note."

On October 10, 2000, Xiqiao Company submitted a Confirmation Letter to the court of first instance, stating: "With respect to the creditor's right of HKD 70 million in the payment supplementary agreement and notes, and the Mortgage Guaranty Contract, Mortgage Guaranty Letter, Guaranty Contract, and other agreements, the creditor's right belongs to Senda Company, which shall assert the right externally. I have no objection." On the same day, Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company submitted an "Explanation of Plaintiffs" to the court of first instance, stating: "The claims of the two companies are consistent, and the creditor's rights of the two plaintiffs are not required to be divided in this case."

At the second-instance hearing, Shanghai Xinjianye Company challenged the authenticity of Li Chen's signature on "Explanatory Note (1)" and orally applied for judicial identification, while promising to submit a written application and prepay the corresponding identification fees within three days after the hearing, failing which the application would be deemed waived. Thereafter, Shanghai Xinjianye Company did not submit a written application for judicial identification to this court, nor did it prepay the corresponding identification fees.

This court holds: At the second instance in this case, after being lawfully summoned, Weicheng Company failed to appear in court without justifiable reasons. Pursuant to Article 4 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, which provides that "any civil litigation conducted within the territory of the People's Republic of China must comply with this Law," Article 157, which provides that "the people's court of second instance shall, unless otherwise provided in this Chapter, apply the ordinary procedure of first instance when hearing appealed cases," and Article 129, which provides that "if a plaintiff, having been served with a summons, refuses to appear in court without justifiable reasons, or withdraws from the court session without the permission of the court, the case may be deemed as withdrawn by the plaintiff; if the defendant files a counterclaim, a judgment by default may be made," it should be held that Weicheng Company has withdrawn its appeal. Therefore, this court will not review the appeal of Weicheng Company.

1. Regarding the issue of the applicable law for the dispute in this case. Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company filed the debt and guarantee dispute lawsuit in the court of first instance based on the payment supplementary agreement and its explanatory notes, the Mortgage Guaranty Contract, the Mortgage Guaranty Letter, and the Guaranty Contract. According to the facts confirmed by the parties at the first instance, the transfer contract was signed between Hong Kong Xinjianye Company, Weicheng Company, and persons not involved in the case, namely Xinjianye Property (Macau) Co., Ltd., Shen Zhubang, Wu Lisheng, and Liang Shusen. The dispute in this case is not a dispute over the transfer contract among the above six parties, but a debt and guarantee dispute between Hong Kong Xinjianye Company, Senda Company, Weicheng Company, and Shanghai Xinjianye Company. Therefore, even if the transfer contract contained provisions on applicable law and jurisdiction, such provisions are not binding on the payment supplementary agreement and the security legal relationships involved in this case.

Pursuant to Article 5 of the Work Memo signed by Xiqiao Company, Senda Company, Xinfa Company, and Shanghai Xinjianye Company, Senda Company and Shanghai Xinjianye Company agreed that all agreements already signed, including the payment supplementary agreement and its explanatory notes, as well as the three security documents, would be governed by Chinese law. Although Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Weicheng Company did not sign the Work Memo, Hong Kong Xinjianye Company, Senda Company, and Weicheng Company, in the "Explanatory Note (2)" signed after the Work Memo, confirmed that the Work Memo and the corresponding security documents complemented the payment supplementary agreement. Therefore, the provision in Article 5 of the Work Memo that "all interpretations of all agreements, contracts, mortgage documents, powers of attorney, etc., shall be finally defined by the Chinese language and Chinese law" is binding on the payment supplementary agreement, its explanatory notes, and the relevant security documents.

Pursuant to Article 5 of the then-effective Law of the People's Republic of China on Economic Contracts Involving Foreign Interest, which provides that "the parties to a contract may choose the law applicable to the settlement of disputes arising from the contract," the resolution of the dispute in this case shall be governed by the laws of the People's Republic of China in accordance with the above agreement. That is, the debt dispute involved in this case shall be handled in accordance with the relevant provisions of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, and the guarantee dispute shall be handled in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Security Law of the People's Republic of China.

2. Regarding the issue of whether Weicheng Company owes a debt to Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company. According to the facts found at first instance, Weicheng Company acknowledged the authenticity of the payment supplementary agreement and its explanatory notes. The original judgment, based on the contents of the payment supplementary agreement and its explanatory notes, as well as Weicheng Company's repayment situation, confirmed that Weicheng Company's actual outstanding debt was HKD 99,344,360.34 (principal). Although Weicheng Company appealed, as it failed to appear in court without reason, it is treated as having withdrawn its appeal. Pursuant to Article 20(1) of the Security Law of the People's Republic of China, which provides that "a surety for general suretyship or joint and several suretyship has the right of defense of the debtor. If the debtor waives its right of defense against the debt, the surety still has the right to defend," Shanghai Xinjianye Company still has the right to defend against whether Weicheng Company owes a debt and the amount of the debt. From the facts already established at both the first and second instances in this case, Shanghai Xinjianye Company has been unable to provide corresponding evidence to overturn the amount of Weicheng Company's debt to Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company as determined in the payment supplementary agreement and its explanatory notes. On the contrary, in the corresponding security documents, Shanghai Xinjianye Company consistently acknowledged Weicheng Company's debt to Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company. At the second-instance hearing, Shanghai Xinjianye Company orally applied for a judicial identification of the authenticity of the signature of Li Chen, who represented Weicheng Company on "Explanatory Note (1)," but Shanghai Xinjianye Company failed to submit a written application and prepay the corresponding identification fees within the promised period, and it should be deemed to have waived its application for judicial identification. The contents of the payment supplementary agreement and its explanatory notes regarding Weicheng Company's debt and repayment plan were consistent with the true intentions of the parties concerned, did not violate the provisions of Chinese laws and regulations, and should be deemed valid. Therefore, Shanghai Xinjianye Company's assertion that the debt of Weicheng Company as determined in the original judgment had no relationship with it or with Weicheng Company lacks factual basis, and this court does not support this assertion. The determination in the original judgment, based on the payment supplementary agreement and its explanatory notes, that Weicheng Company still owed Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company HKD 99,344,360.34 is confirmed by this court.

3. Regarding the validity of the guarantee involved in this case. Shanghai Xinjianye Company issued a total of three guarantee documents for Weicheng Company, including the Mortgage Guarantee Contract, the Mortgage Guarantee Letter, and the Guarantee Contract. The judgment of the first instance found that the Mortgage Guarantee Contract and the Mortgage Guarantee Letter were invalid due to failure to complete mortgage registration procedures, which is correct. Shanghai Xinjianye Company appealed, arguing that the first instance judgment erroneously found that "after the mortgage contract was signed, the mortgage registration procedures have not been completed to date, therefore the mortgage contract has not taken effect, and the existing evidence cannot prove that either party to the contract was at fault for its non-effectiveness, and Shanghai Xinjianye Company shall bear joint and several liability for repayment." However, upon verification, the first instance judgment did not make such a finding; Shanghai Xinjianye Company misquoted the first instance judgment, which actually found that "this contract has no legal binding force on either party." The first instance judgment did not order Shanghai Xinjianye Company to bear liability because the mortgage guarantee was found invalid. Regarding the validity of the Guarantee Contract, Shanghai Xinjianye Company mainly raised the following contentions: (1) Shen Zhubang, as a director of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, provided a guarantee for Weicheng Company, which is a shareholder of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, and therefore the guarantee contract should be found invalid; (2) Shen Zhubang simultaneously represented both Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Shanghai Xinjianye Company in signing the Guarantee Contract, constituting "dual agency," which harmed the legitimate rights and interests of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, and the Guarantee Contract should be found invalid; (3) When Shen Zhubang signed the Guarantee Contract, he had already been removed from his position as Chairman of the Board of Directors of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, thus he had no authority to sign the Guarantee Contract on behalf of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, and the Guarantee Contract is not binding on Shanghai Xinjianye Company; (4) The Guarantee Contract should be found invalid for lack of approval and registration.

This Court is of the opinion that the grounds on which Shanghai Xinjianye Company contends that the Guarantee Contract is invalid have no legal basis: (1) According to the facts found in the first instance and on appeal, Shanghai Xinjianye Company is a wholly foreign-owned enterprise established in Shanghai in 1994 by Xinfa Company. Although Weicheng Company became the controlling shareholder of Xinfa Company through a transfer agreement, Weicheng Company is not a shareholder of Shanghai Xinjianye Company. Therefore, Shanghai Xinjianye Company's provision of a guarantee to Weicheng Company is not subject to the restriction of Article 60, paragraph 3 of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China, which provides that "directors and managers shall not use company assets to provide guarantees for the company's shareholders or other individuals' debts." (2) According to the relevant provisions of Chinese laws and regulations, an enterprise that meets the conditions for being an enterprise legal person, upon approval by the state-authorized examination and approval authority or competent department and registration by the registration authority, the principal responsible person who exercises powers on behalf of the legal person is the legal representative of the enterprise legal person. Current Chinese laws and regulations do not prohibit an individual from simultaneously serving as the legal representative of two or more enterprise legal persons, nor do they restrict enterprise legal persons with the same legal representative from engaging in civil juristic acts. Therefore, Shen Zhubang, as the legal representative of both Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Shanghai Xinjianye Company at that time, signing the Guarantee Contract on behalf of both companies simultaneously does not violate current Chinese laws and regulations. (3) The Guarantee Contract was signed by Shen Zhubang on behalf of Shanghai Xinjianye Company with relevant parties on February 25, 1997. It is true that Shen Zhubang was removed from his position as Chairman of the Board of Directors of Shanghai Xinjianye Company by a resolution of the company's board of directors on January 18, 1997. On June 27 of the same year, after industrial and commercial registration, the legal representative of Shanghai Xinjianye Company was changed from Shen Zhubang to Yin Jun. Article 3 of the Provisions on the Administration of Registration of Legal Representatives of Enterprise Legal Persons, issued by the State Administration for Industry and Commerce on April 7, 1998, with the approval of the State Council, provides that "the legal representative of an enterprise legal person, upon registration by the enterprise registration authority, obtains the qualification of legal representative." Therefore, before the enterprise registration authority made a change in the registration of the legal representative of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, Shen Zhubang remained the legal representative of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, and he had the authority to sign relevant documents on behalf of Shanghai Xinjianye Company externally. Although the guarantee matter involved in the Guarantee Contract was not approved by a resolution of the board of directors of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, this case has certain peculiarities, namely, there is a certain connection among the creditor, debtor, and guarantor. In particular, there is a considerable overlap of board members between the creditor and the guarantor. Most of the directors of Shanghai Xinjianye Company had already signed relevant agreements agreeing that Shanghai Xinjianye Company would act as the repayment guarantor for Weicheng Company, and Shanghai Xinjianye Company never raised any objection to the guarantee matter before the dispute in this case arose. Therefore, it can be found that the signing of the Guarantee Contract did not harm the interests of Shanghai Xinjianye Company and was consistent with the genuine intent of Shanghai Xinjianye Company. As for the issue of the "contract seal" of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, since Shen Zhubang had the authority to sign documents on behalf of the company externally, whether the "contract seal" was concealed or forged does not affect the validity of the Guarantee Contract. (4) Article 8, paragraph 2 of the Detailed Rules for the Implementation of the Measures for the Administration of External Guarantees by Domestic Institutions provides: "Wholly foreign-owned enterprises may voluntarily provide external guarantees without the need for case-by-case approval from the foreign exchange bureau." According to the above provision, as a wholly foreign-owned enterprise, Shanghai Xinjianye Company does not need approval from the foreign exchange bureau to provide a guarantee for Weicheng Company.

In summary, the Guarantee Contract signed by Shanghai Xinjianye Company with Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company reflects the genuine intent of Shanghai Xinjianye Company. Shanghai Xinjianye Company has no evidence to prove that there were circumstances of fraud or malicious collusion among the relevant parties that harmed its legitimate rights and interests. The Guarantee Contract also does not violate the prohibitive provisions of current Chinese laws and regulations and should be found valid. Since the parties did not agree on the method of guarantee in the guarantee contract, according to Article 19 of the Security Law of the People's Republic of China, which provides that "if the parties have not agreed on the method of guarantee or the agreement is not clear, the guarantor shall bear the guarantee liability as a joint and several liability guarantor," Shanghai Xinjianye Company shall bear joint and several liability for repayment for Weicheng Company's debts involved in this case. The finding of the first instance judgment regarding the nature of the Guarantee Contract is correct.

4. Regarding the provisions on repayment guarantee in the Supplementary Payment Agreement. The Supplementary Payment Agreement actually stipulated two parts: one is the repayment plan, and the other is Weicheng Company's use of the "Shanghai Xinjianye Center" as a repayment guarantee. Since the "Shanghai Xinjianye Center" is an asset of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, although Weicheng Company had become the controlling shareholder of Xinfa Company, and Xinfa Company is a shareholder of Shanghai Xinjianye Company, Shanghai Xinjianye Company is an independent Chinese enterprise legal person. Weicheng Company has no right to dispose of the assets of Shanghai Xinjianye Company. Therefore, the provision in Article 1, paragraph 1 of the Supplementary Payment Agreement, that "Weicheng Company uses the Shanghai Xinjianye Center as a repayment guarantee," is invalid, and Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company have no priority right to be satisfied from the "Shanghai Xinjianye Center."

5. Regarding the finding of the first instance judgment that "the creditor uses the subject matter it has transferred as a guarantee." This Court is of the opinion that this finding is erroneous. First, the court of first instance had no jurisdiction over the transfer agreement. Second, in the transfer agreement, the subject matter transferred was the shares of Hong Kong Xinjianye Company in Xinfa Company, while the collateral provided by Shanghai Xinjianye Company was the "Shanghai Xinjianye Center," which is an asset of Shanghai Xinjianye Company; the two are not the same. The only connection is that Hong Kong Xinjianye Company was originally a shareholder of Xinfa Company, and Xinfa Company is a shareholder of Shanghai Xinjianye Company. However, the assets owned by each of these three companies are independent and cannot be commingled or disposed of by proxy.

6. Regarding the calculation of interest. The Supplementary Payment Agreement only stipulated the final date for repayment, i.e., July 22, 1997, but did not provide for interest on overdue payments. Weicheng Company failed to pay the debt as stipulated in the Supplementary Payment Agreement and shall bear liability for breach of contract. The first instance judgment ordering Weicheng Company to pay interest for the period during which the funds were occupied without compensation is correct. Shanghai Xinjianye Company's appeal arguing that interest should not be calculated has no factual or legal basis.

7. Regarding the respective shares of the claims between Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company. During the first instance proceedings, Hong Kong Xinjianye Company and Senda Company explicitly stated that they would not divide the total claim in this case. This Court confirms this.

In summary, the facts found by the first instance judgment are basically clear, and the law applied is correct. The judgment result should be upheld. The appeal by appellant Shanghai Xinjianye Company is without merit and should be dismissed; appellant Weicheng Company, after being properly served by this Court, refused to appear in court to participate in the proceedings, and its appeal is treated as withdrawn. Pursuant to Articles 157, 129, and 153(1)(1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this Court hereby renders the following judgment:

1. The appeal of Xinjianye Real Estate Development (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. is dismissed.

2. The appeal of Hong Kong Weicheng International Co., Ltd. is treated as withdrawn.

3. The civil judgment (1999) Hu Gao Jing Chu Zi No. 4 of the Shanghai High People's Court is affirmed.

The court acceptance fee and property preservation fee for the first instance shall be borne as determined in the first instance judgment; the court acceptance fee for the second instance of RMB 754,799.89 shall be borne by Xinjianye Real Estate Development (Shanghai) Co., Ltd.

This judgment is final.
